title: Girl, Interrupted by Martyna Majok and Aimee Mann at The Public #girl...
transcript: Stephen Sondheim said content should dictate form, and Girl, Interrupted is a perfect example of this. Based on a memoir of the same name, Susanna Kaysen reflects on the time she spent at McLean Hospital, a mental institution that also treated famous figures such as James Taylor and Sylvia Plath. During her stay, Susanna forms unexpected and profound connections with the other patients, exemplifying how it's the places we least expect where we find the people who understand us the most. I'd say that's the primary takeaway, but the piece touches on a lot of other ideas, too. Despite it featuring primarily female characters, patriarchy looms large like the cage floating above the stage the entire time. I was also left thinking about what we define as “insane” or “crazy” and the sometimes predatory nature of healthcare. In line with the subject matter and the original format of the story, there's not really a traditional narrative arc. Though it's presented through a linear timeline, it feels amorphous along the way and you never know exactly where it's going or when we're going to turn a corner to a significant revelation. It's appropriately stark and claustrophobic, being a lengthy single act with no real indication of when or how things are going to resolve. Over time, I was able to sink in and let it wash over me, and I grew less resistant to this ambiguity in a way that was perhaps designed to loosely mirror the experience of our narrator. With this in mind, I could forgive the occasional slow point in the play, especially knowing the story wasn't originally written to fit a traditional theatrical structure. It also helped that the writing is strong — there's an eloquence and specificity to Martyna Majok's prose that's at odds with what you might expect from the patients of a psychiatric hospital but is actually what excavates deep emotional truths out of every character. Even more memorable are the absolutely stunning arrangements and vocal performances of the songs by Aimee Mann. This is a case where I might attend the show again simply because there's so much to notice and pick apart, but above all else, I would love a cast recording. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
classificationReason: Creator shares a detailed first-hand critical opinion of the Public Theatre production — discussing narrative structure, staging ('a cage floating above the stage'), themes, and form. Clear personal attendance ('I was also left thinking...').
